title: A Linear Model's Out-of-Fold Disagreements Find the Flipped Labels: Filtering Label Noise Without a Clean Set or a Noise Rate
insight: Under symmetric label noise, the samples that a logistic regression fit on other folds cannot explain are mostly the mislabeled ones, so dropping them and refitting recovers accuracy and beats a larger MLP trained on the same noisy labels.
abstract_sketch: Methods that clean noisy labels usually need a clean validation set, a noise-rate estimate, or a deep network, and it is unclear how far a plain linear model gets without them. We measure one simple rule: fit logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation on the noisy labels, drop every training sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its label, and refit on the rest. The rule works because a sample that a model fit on other folds cannot explain is more likely mislabeled than one it explains. On two small datasets with symmetric noise at 20 and 40%, most dropped samples are truly mislabeled and most flipped labels are dropped, the refit model beats plain logistic regression in 19 of 20 paired runs, and it beats an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels in all 20. With clean labels the filter costs a fraction of a point and the MLP is as good or slightly better. This is a small study, and we make no claim about deep networks, large data, or other noise types.
figure1: Three panels, with the evidence in the third. Panel 1 (numbered circle 1, 'Noisy labels'): a small grid of training samples with a few flipped labels marked in red. Panel 2 (circle 2, 'Out-of-fold check'): five folds, each predicted by a model fit on the other four; samples whose prediction disagrees with the given label are crossed out, and the crossed-out set is shown as a stacked bar split into truly flipped and clean-but-dropped (mean precision above 50% in all four noisy cells, recall 79 to 98%). Panel 3 (circle 3, 'Refit'): grouped bars of test accuracy at 0, 20 and 40% noise for logistic regression (muted hue), MLP (second muted hue), and the filter (Northwestern purple), mean over 5 seeds with seed points and sd error bars, digits shown in the main figure and breast cancer in the supplement or a second small group. The reader sees that the purple bars stay near the 0% level while the baselines fall, and that the MLP falls furthest. The caption states the cases are means over all seeds, not selected.
contributions: We show that out-of-fold disagreement of a logistic regression is a reliable detector of flipped labels under symmetric noise: most dropped samples are truly mislabeled and most flipped labels are dropped, in every noisy setting we ran.

We present a filter that fits logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation, drops disagreeing samples and refits, needing no clean validation set and using no noise rate, and show that it beats plain logistic regression and an untuned 64-unit MLP under 20 and 40% noise.

We report where it does not help and what it costs: a small loss on clean labels, a tie with the MLP on clean data, an unstable breast cancer cell at 40% noise, about five times the fit time, and a scope limited to two small datasets and symmetric noise.
storyline: A linear model fit on noisy labels loses many accuracy points, and a small MLP trained on the same labels loses far more. We open with the cleanest measurement in the study: when a logistic regression predicts each training sample from folds that exclude it, the samples it disagrees with are mostly the flipped ones, in every noisy setting and with tests against 50% precision all clearly significant. This is the reason a filter works: a sample that other folds cannot explain is more likely mislabeled than one they explain, and the rule needs neither a clean validation set nor a noise rate. Dropping those samples and refitting beats plain logistic regression in nearly every paired run and beats the MLP in every one, with gains that grow with the noise rate on digits. It recovers most of the lost accuracy in three of four noisy settings and little in the unstable breast cancer 40% setting. On clean labels the cost is a fraction of a point and the MLP ties or slightly wins. What this changes: before reaching for a bigger model or a noise-rate estimate, a linear model's own out-of-fold errors already clean most of the noise, at least on small tabular-scale problems.

sections.title: Most samples the filter drops are truly mislabeled, and most flipped labels are dropped
Filtering beats plain logistic regression under noise, with larger gains at higher noise

risks: A reviewer will say the study is tiny (two small datasets, five seeds, one noise type) and that confident learning and co-teaching are not compared. The paper answers by stating the scope in the abstract and limitations, citing those methods as related work only, and noting that confident learning also uses out-of-fold predictions, so what is new is the plain, checkable measurement for a linear model rather than the idea of cross-validated noise detection. The MLP is untuned and its poor noisy accuracy is not explained by an experiment (memorization is only consistent with it), so the MLP comparison is worded as against an untuned MLP. The recovery share is our own definition and is partial on breast cancer at 40% noise, where seed variance is about 9 points; we report that cell with its limit. The filter ties or loses slightly on clean data, which five seeds cannot prove equivalent, and it costs about five times the fit time.

skim.read: Fitting logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation on noisy labels, dropping samples whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with their label, and refitting on the rest identifies most flipped labels and, on two small datasets with symmetric noise, gives better test accuracy than plain logistic regression (19 of 20 paired runs) and an untuned MLP (20 of 20), without needing a clean set or a noise rate.
skim.why: Same method, finding (identifies flipped labels, beats LR and MLP under symmetric noise); summary adds specific scope details but is consistent.
